mcq.q: Two vectors point the same way but one is twice as long. Which is unchanged?
options: Dot product
Euclidean distance
Cosine similarity
Both norms
mcq.why: Cosine normalises by length, so scaling one vector leaves it unchanged.
distractors: The dot product scales with length, so doubling one vector doubles it.
The distance between the vectors' tips grows when one of them gets longer.
One norm doubles; only the angle between the vectors is unchanged.

mcq.q: What is the cosine similarity of [1, 0] and [1, 1]?
options: About 0.71
About 1.41
distractors: 0.5 is cos 60°, not 45°.
1.41 is √2, the length of b; cosine is never above 1.
1.0 would mean the same direction.

mcq.q: What is the dot product of [2, 1, 0] and [1, 3, 4]?
distractors: That adds the products wrongly; the last term is 0·4 = 0.
That adds all the entries instead of multiplying pairs.
Only one pair multiplies to zero.

mcq.q: What is the norm (length) of [3, 4]?
distractors: 7 adds the entries.
12 multiplies the entries.
25 is the squared length, before the square root.

mcq.q: Why do vector databases usually normalise embeddings to length 1?
options: So the embedding model can be swapped without re-embedding documents
So each vector takes less disk space once its length is fixed
So every similarity score comes out positive and easy to rank
So cosine similarity equals the cheaper dot product
mcq.why: For unit vectors, a·b = cos θ, so ranking by dot product gives cosine ranking at lower cost.
distractors: Vectors from another model live in a different space; normalising does not make them comparable.
A unit vector has as many dimensions, and bytes, as before.
Unit vectors can still point apart: cosine still ranges from −1 to 1.

mcq.q: What is the projection of a = [2, 2] onto b = [1, 0]?
mcq.why: (a·b / ‖b‖²)·b = (2/1)·[1, 0] = [2, 0]: the part of a that points along b.
distractors: That halves a; it is not a projection onto b.
That is a itself.
That is the part of a perpendicular to b.

mcq.q: A cosine similarity of 0 means the two vectors are…
options: Identical, pointing the same way with equal length
Opposite, pointing in exactly reverse directions
Both zero vectors, since they share nothing
Perpendicular, so unrelated in that space
mcq.why: Cosine 1 means same direction, 0 perpendicular, −1 opposite.
distractors: Vectors pointing the same way have cosine 1.
Opposite directions give cosine −1.
Cosine with a zero vector is undefined, not 0.

mcq.q: Multiplying one token's vector by a 4096 × 4096 weight matrix takes about how many multiply-adds?
options: About 67 million
About 8.2 thousand
About 16.7 million
About 4.1 thousand
mcq.why: Each of the 4,096 outputs is a dot product of length 4,096: 4,096² ≈ 16.7 million multiply-adds.
distractors: Four times too many: there is one multiply-add per weight, 4096 × 4096 ≈ 16.7 million.
8,192 is 4096 + 4096: it adds the dimensions instead of multiplying them.
4,096 is one output's dot product; there are 4,096 outputs, each needing 4,096 multiply-adds.

mcq.q: An embedding call failed and your code stored a zero vector. What happens when you compute its cosine similarity?
options: It is 1, because a zero vector matches every direction equally
It is −1, because the zero vector points away from every document
It is undefined (division by zero), so NaN scores can reach ranking
It is 0, which ranks the document last and is therefore safe
mcq.why: Cosine divides by both norms; a zero norm makes it undefined. Detect failed or empty embeddings explicitly.
distractors: Cosine divides by both norms; a zero norm makes it undefined, not 1.
A zero vector has no direction, so it cannot point away from anything.
0/0 is undefined; libraries return NaN, which can break sorting and ranking.

mcq.q: A neural network layer is mostly…
options: A sorting step
A matrix multiplication
A lookup table of facts
A set of IF–THEN rules
mcq.why: A layer multiplies its input by a weight matrix (plus a bias and an activation), which is why AI hardware is built around fast matrix multiplication.
distractors: Layers do not sort.
Facts are not stored as lookups.
Rules are hand-written; layers are learned weights.

interview.q: Explain the dot product, the norm and cosine similarity, and when you would use each.
covers: Dot product measures alignment and grows with length
Cosine is the angle only, from 1 to −1
Cosine compares meaning when length is irrelevant
For unit vectors, cosine equals the dot product
interview.followUp: Your embeddings are not normalised. Which of the three would you use for retrieval, and why?

interview.q: Why is a matrix multiplication “many dot products at once”, and why does that matter for hardware?
covers: Each output is a row-by-vector dot product
Huge numbers of identical operations parallelise well
GPUs and their matrix units are built for this
interview.followUp: How many multiply-adds does one 4096 × 4096 layer take for a single token?

interview.q: What does it mean for embeddings to be normalised, and why do vector stores do it?
covers: Cosine then equals the dot product
Removes length effects that do not carry meaning
interview.followUp: What goes wrong if only some vectors in the store are normalised?

interview.q: Your retrieval returns NaN scores for some documents. What would you check?
covers: Zero or empty vectors from failed embedding calls
Wrong data types or corrupted values
interview.followUp: How would you stop zero vectors from reaching the store in the first place?

interview.q: How do you choose between cosine similarity, dot product and Euclidean distance for retrieval?
covers: What the embedding model was trained with
interview.followUp: The model card says it was trained with dot product on unnormalised vectors. Does that change your choice?

interview.q: {company}'s “similar products” row shows unrelated items for some listings. How would you debug it with vector maths?
covers: Check normalisation and that all vectors come from the same model version
Look for short or empty titles producing weak vectors
Inspect the cosine values of the nearest neighbours
Set a minimum similarity before showing anything
interview.followUp: What minimum similarity would you set, and how would you choose it?

interview.q: Design an embedding pipeline that keeps vectors comparable across re-indexing.
covers: Store the model name and version with each vector
Normalise and validate (dimension, non-zero) at write time
Re-embed everything when the model changes
Never mix versions in one index
Tests on known similar and dissimilar pairs
interview.followUp: How would you migrate a live index to a new embedding model without downtime?

interview.q: How would you reduce the cost of similarity search over ten million vectors?
interview.followUp: How would you know the approximate index is not missing good results?

mcq.q: A detector has 95% recall and 1% false positives; the condition occurs in 0.1% of cases. Most alerts are…
options: true positives
false positives
impossible to estimate
exactly half true
mcq.why: With a 0.1% base rate, false alarms from the 99.9% negatives vastly outnumber true detections (Bayes).
distractors: With a 0.1% base rate there are about 10 false alerts for every true one.
Recall, the false-positive rate and the base rate are enough to count both kinds of alert.
Per 100,000 cases: about 95 true alerts and about 1,000 false ones, nowhere near half.

mcq.q: A prompt passes 86 of 100 test cases. Roughly what is the 95% confidence interval for its pass rate?
options: About 78% to 91%
Exactly 86%
About 50% to 100%
About 85% to 87%
mcq.why: With only 100 cases the Wilson interval is roughly 78%–91%, so a 4-point difference from another prompt is within noise.
distractors: A sample gives an estimate, not the exact rate.
That is far too wide for 100 cases.
That interval is far too narrow for 100 cases.

mcq.q: To halve the width of a confidence interval for a pass rate, you need about…
options: Four times as many test cases
The same number, run twice
Twice as many test cases
Half as many test cases
mcq.why: Interval width shrinks with √n, so halving it needs four times the cases.
distractors: Rerunning the same cases does not add information about new inputs.
Doubling cases shrinks the width by only about 30%.
Fewer cases widen the interval.

mcq.q: A fraud model has 95% recall and a 2% false-positive rate, and 0.5% of transactions are fraud. Roughly what share of flagged transactions are fraud?
options: About 95%
About 50%
About 2%
About 19%
mcq.why: Per 1,000 transactions: 5 are fraud and 4.75 are caught; 995 are genuine and 19.9 are flagged. 4.75 ÷ 24.65 ≈ 19%.
distractors: 95% is the recall, not the precision.
That ignores the base rate.
2% is the false-positive rate.

mcq.q: What does P(A | B) mean?
options: The probability of A given that B is true
A divided by B
The probability of B given A
The probability of A and B both being true
mcq.why: It is a conditional probability. Bayes' theorem turns P(B | A) into P(A | B) using the base rate.
distractors: It is not a ratio of the events.
That is the reverse conditional, which Bayes' theorem converts.
That is the joint probability P(A and B).

mcq.q: Language modelling estimates which probability?
options: P(next token | previous tokens)
P(document is true)
P(user is satisfied)
P(previous tokens | next token)
mcq.why: A language model gives a conditional distribution over the next token given the text so far.
distractors: Truth is not what the model estimates.
Satisfaction is a product metric, not the model's output.
That is the reverse direction.

mcq.q: Why is a paired comparison more powerful when two models ran on the same test cases?
options: It doubles the sample size, because each case is counted once per model
It compares per-case differences, so the variation in case difficulty cancels out
It lifts both models' scores, because each case is scored twice
It removes the need for a test set, since the models check each other
mcq.why: Counting cases where only one model passed (a sign or McNemar test) focuses on the actual differences between them.
distractors: The number of independent cases is the same; pairing removes noise, it does not add cases.
Pairing changes the analysis, not the scores.
You still need test cases; pairing is how you compare results on them.

mcq.q: You compute a tight confidence interval from a sample of only English tickets and report it for all traffic. What is the problem?
options: Confidence intervals are valid only for English text, not other languages
The sample is biased, so the interval can be precisely wrong about real traffic
The interval is too wide to use, because English tickets vary so much
Nothing: a tight interval holds for all traffic once the sample is large
mcq.why: An interval reflects sampling noise, not bias. A sample that does not represent traffic gives a confident wrong answer.
distractors: The maths does not depend on language; the problem is which cases were sampled.
The interval was tight; a tight interval around a biased estimate is the danger.
An interval covers sampling noise, not bias from an unrepresentative sample.

mcq.q: Under the method's assumptions, a 95% confidence interval is a range that…
options: Contains 95% of the individual data points in the sample
Would contain the true value in about 95% of repeated experiments
Has a 95% chance of being wrong about the true value
Is always centred on the true value, give or take a little
mcq.why: It quantifies how far the estimate could be off because you only tested a sample.
distractors: That describes the spread of the data, not the uncertainty of an estimate.
The other way round: about 95% of such intervals cover the true value.
It is centred on the estimate; the true value is unknown.

mcq.q: In evaluation, what is being sampled?
options: Test cases drawn from all possible inputs
The model's weights, drawn fresh for each run
Random seeds, one for each evaluation run
Tokens drawn from the model's vocabulary
mcq.why: An evaluation set is a sample of possible inputs, which is why results carry uncertainty.
distractors: Weights are fixed during an evaluation.
Seeds affect decoding; the sample that sets an interval's width is the test cases.
Picking tokens is decoding, not the evaluation sample.

interview.q: Explain Bayes' theorem using an alert or fraud example.
covers: Precision can be low even with high recall
interview.followUp: How would you explain to a manager why a 99%-accurate detector raises mostly false alarms?

interview.q: What is a confidence interval, and what does it not tell you?
covers: Does not cover bias or an unrepresentative sample
Not the probability the true value lies in this specific interval
interview.followUp: How would you make the interval half as wide?

interview.q: Why do base rates matter when you judge a detector?
covers: Rare positives mean most alerts can be false
Operational load follows from alerts per day
interview.followUp: The team can review only 200 alerts a day. How do you set the threshold?

interview.q: A new prompt scores 86% and the old one 82% on the same 100 cases. Is the new one better?
covers: Use a paired comparison on the same cases
Get more cases, or accept uncertainty explicitly
interview.followUp: How many cases would you want, and why?

interview.q: How many test cases do you need to detect a two-point improvement?
interview.followUp: Labelling is expensive. How would you get the same power from fewer labelled cases?

interview.q: {company}'s fraud model has 90% recall and 2% false positives. Roughly how many alerts a day does it raise on one million transactions, and what does that mean for the team?
covers: Base rate about 1.4%: about 12,600 frauds caught
About 32,000 alerts a day at roughly 39% precision
Analysts needed follows from minutes per alert
Set the threshold to an alert budget instead
interview.followUp: The team can review 2,000 alerts a day. What do you change?

interview.q: Design an evaluation report a manager can trust when comparing two models.
interview.followUp: The new model wins overall but loses on one slice. What do you recommend?

interview.q: A data-leak alert fires mostly false alarms. How would you redesign it?
covers: Route alerts to review instead of blocking
Two-stage detection: cheap filter then precise check
Measure and tune with labelled outcomes
interview.followUp: How would you measure whether the redesign helped?

mcq.q: A model assigns probability 0.1 to the correct token. Its cross-entropy loss is about…
options: 0.10 nats
0.69 nats
2.30 nats
10 nats
mcq.why: Loss = −ln(0.1) ≈ 2.30 nats.
distractors: 0.1 is the probability itself, not its negative log.
0.69 nats is −ln 0.5, the loss at probability 0.5.
10 nats would mean a probability of about 0.00005.

mcq.q: What is the entropy of a fair coin, in bits?
options: 1 bit
0.5 bits
0 bits
2 bits
distractors: That halves the correct value.
0 bits is a coin that always lands the same way.
2 bits would need four equally likely outcomes.

mcq.q: For a language model with a 50,000-token vocabulary, what should the first training-step loss be near?
options: About 1 nat
About 10.8 nats
About 50,000 nats
About 4.7 nats
mcq.why: An untrained model is close to uniform, so the loss is ln(50,000) ≈ 10.8.
distractors: A loss of 1 means probability about 0.37 on the real token, far better than a random start.
50,000 is the vocabulary size; the loss is its log, ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8.
4.7 is log base 10 of 50,000; losses use the natural log.

mcq.q: When the true distribution puts all its mass on the real next token, cross-entropy reduces to…
options: log q(real token)
The entropy of q
−log q(real token)
Zero, since p is certain
mcq.why: With p = 1 on the real token, H(p, q) = −log q(real token).
distractors: Without the minus sign the loss would be negative; −log q(real) is positive.
The entropy of q ignores which token was real.
The entropy of p is zero, but cross-entropy is −log q(real token), zero only if q gives that token probability 1.

mcq.q: Which statement about KL divergence KL(p‖q) is correct?
options: It equals the cross-entropy H(p,q), including the entropy of p
It is symmetric, so KL(p‖q) always equals KL(q‖p)
It is H(p,q) − H(p), never negative, and zero only when q = p
It can be negative when q fits the data better than p
mcq.why: KL is the extra surprise from using q instead of p.
distractors: KL is cross-entropy minus the entropy of p.
KL is asymmetric; swapping p and q gives a different value.
KL is never negative, and zero only when the distributions match.

mcq.q: Where is KL divergence used when tuning LLMs?
options: To choose the tokenizer that gives the lowest loss on a corpus
To keep a tuned model close to its original in RLHF and DPO
To set the context window from the length of the training data
To measure how far apart two embeddings are in a vector store
mcq.why: A KL term penalises drifting too far from the reference model while optimising rewards or preferences (6.5).
distractors: Tokenizers are built from merge rules on a corpus, not chosen by KL.
Context length is an architecture and training choice.
Vector stores use cosine or dot product between vectors; KL compares probability distributions.

mcq.q: A model's average loss is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity?
options: About 7.4
About 0.13
mcq.why: Perplexity = e^loss = e² ≈ 7.4: roughly the number of tokens it is choosing between.
distractors: That would be 10², using the wrong base.
That is e^−2.
That is the loss itself.

mcq.q: A model gives the correct answer only 1% probability. What is its loss on that example?
options: About 4.6 nats
About 0.01 nats
About 1 nat
About 46 nats
mcq.why: −ln 0.01 ≈ 4.6. Being confidently wrong is expensive.
distractors: 0.01 is the probability; the loss is −ln 0.01.
A loss of 1 corresponds to probability about 0.37.
ln 100 is 4.6, not 46: a misplaced decimal point.

mcq.q: A model improves perplexity but fails critical extraction cases. What should you conclude?
options: Lower token loss does not guarantee task success; evaluate the task directly
The model is now strictly better, since perplexity improved overall
The extraction tests must be wrong, because perplexity says it improved
Perplexity is the only metric that matters for a language model's quality
mcq.why: Perplexity measures average next-token prediction; specific tasks need their own evaluation.
distractors: Average token loss can improve while the tokens that matter for the task get worse.
The tests measure the task; perplexity measures next-token prediction in general.
Perplexity is a training signal; usefulness is measured on the task.

mcq.q: What is the entropy of a coin that always lands heads?
options: 0.5 bits
1 bit
Infinite
mcq.why: There is no surprise, so the entropy is 0.
distractors: There is no uncertainty to measure.
1 bit is a fair coin.
Entropy is finite; it is 0 here.

interview.q: Explain entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence in plain terms.
covers: Entropy: average surprise of a distribution
Cross-entropy: surprise when predicting with q
KL: the extra surprise from using q instead of p
KL is never negative and zero only when they match
interview.followUp: Why is KL divergence not a distance, and when does that matter?

interview.q: Why is cross-entropy the training loss for language models?
covers: It rewards probability on the real next token
interview.followUp: What happens to the loss when the model puts almost zero probability on the real token?

interview.q: What is perplexity, and how do you read it?
covers: Roughly the number of choices the model is hedging between
Only comparable with the same tokenizer and data
interview.followUp: A model's perplexity is 8. What does that tell you, and what does it not?

interview.q: Your first training-step loss is far from ln(vocabulary size). What might be wrong?
covers: Data leakage making it too low
interview.followUp: What would you do in the first ten minutes?

interview.q: Two models report different perplexities. Can you say which is better?
covers: Only with the same tokenizer and evaluation text
Per-token loss depends on token size
Normalise per character or byte if needed
interview.followUp: How would you compare them fairly if their tokenizers differ?

interview.q: How would you use KL divergence to detect a shift in where {company}'s customers book?
covers: Compare against the same season last year
Check the forecast models when it fires
interview.followUp: The alert fires every December. How do you stop that from being a false alarm?

interview.q: Design a monitoring check that compares this week's inputs with the training data.
covers: An action when it fires: measure performance, not retrain blindly
interview.followUp: The check fires but accuracy has not dropped. What do you do?

interview.q: Explain how a KL penalty keeps an RLHF- or DPO-tuned model from drifting, and what goes wrong without it.
covers: Reward or preference optimisation alone can exploit the reward
KL to a reference model limits the drift
Its weight trades reward against staying close
Without it: degenerate or unsafe outputs
interview.followUp: How would you choose the weight of the KL penalty?

mcq.q: In gradient descent, why do we step against the gradient?
options: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase
Stepping against it makes the effective learning rate larger
The gradient points towards the minimum along the shortest path
The gradient is always negative, so subtracting it moves weights up
mcq.why: ∇L points uphill, so θ ← θ − η·∇L moves downhill.
distractors: The learning rate is set separately; the sign only chooses the direction.
It points to the steepest local increase, away from lower loss.
Its sign varies by parameter and by position on the surface.

mcq.q: For L(w) = (w − 3)², what is dL/dw at w = 1?
distractors: The derivative is 0 only at the minimum, w = 3.
That has the wrong sign: w is below 3, so the slope is negative.
That forgets the factor of 2.

mcq.q: For L(w) = (w − 3)², learning rate 0.1, starting at w = 1, what is w after one step?
mcq.why: w ← 1 − 0.1·(−4) = 1.4: a step towards the minimum at 3.
distractors: That adds the gradient instead of subtracting it.
That uses a gradient of −1.
One small step does not reach the minimum.

mcq.q: For y = (3x)², what is dy/dx at x = 2?
mcq.why: With u = 3x: dy/du = 2u = 12 and du/dx = 3, so dy/dx = 12 × 3 = 36.
distractors: That uses 2u with u = 3.
That is only dy/du.
That is u, not a derivative.

mcq.q: What happens when the learning rate is too large?
options: The model stops using gradients and falls back to random steps
Training gets slower but always converges in the end
Nothing changes, because the optimiser rescales every step anyway
Steps overshoot: the loss oscillates or explodes, often to NaN
mcq.why: Too large a step jumps past the minimum and can grow each time.
distractors: It still follows gradients; the steps are just too big.
Too-large steps can make the loss oscillate or diverge.
Plain SGD does not rescale steps, and even Adam diverges with a large enough rate.

mcq.q: Backpropagation is…
options: The chain rule applied through every layer
A method for picking the learning rate of each layer
A data-cleaning step that removes noisy labels
A decoding strategy that revisits earlier tokens
mcq.why: Each operation only needs its local derivative; the framework multiplies them on the way back.
distractors: Learning rates come from tuning and schedules.
Backpropagation computes gradients; it does not touch the data.
Decoding is inference; backpropagation is part of training.

mcq.q: Training loss falls steadily while validation loss rises. What does that show?
options: Training is working well, since training loss is what matters
The learning rate is too small to make progress on new data
The model is overfitting: it is not generalising
The validation set is too big for the model to learn in time
mcq.why: Falling training loss alone is not proof of learning; validation loss shows generalisation.
distractors: Validation loss is what shows whether the model generalises.
A small rate slows the training loss too; this pattern is overfitting.
The model never trains on the validation set.

mcq.q: In the 3D figure, why can momentum roll through a small dip that stops plain SGD?
options: It uses a larger loss value to push past the dip
It ignores the gradient while it is inside a small dip
It keeps a running velocity from earlier steps
It sees the whole surface and skips over local dips
mcq.why: Momentum accumulates past gradients, so it keeps moving across small flat or uphill stretches.
distractors: Momentum does not change the loss.
It still uses the gradient, adding it to its velocity.
Optimisers only see the local gradient.

mcq.q: What does Adam do differently from plain SGD?
options: Computes exact second derivatives for every parameter at each step
Updates only one randomly chosen parameter per step to save memory
Uses no learning rate, since it estimates the best step size itself
Scales each parameter's step by a running estimate of its gradient size
mcq.why: Dividing by the running gradient size gives each parameter a similar pace, whatever its slope.
distractors: Adam keeps running averages of gradients and squared gradients, not exact second derivatives.
Adam updates every parameter at each step.
Adam still has a learning rate; it scales it per parameter.

mcq.q: For L(w) = (w − 3)² with learning rate 1.1, starting at w = 1, what happens?
options: It converges smoothly to 3, just more slowly than with 0.1
It stays at w = 1, because the gradient there is too small
It oscillates around 3 with growing amplitude and diverges
It reaches 3 in one step, since 1.1 is close to the ideal rate
mcq.why: Each step multiplies the distance from 3 by (1 − 2η) = −1.2: 1, 5.4, 0.12… the error grows and flips sign.
distractors: Each step multiplies the distance from 3 by (1 − 2·1.1) = −1.2, so it grows.
The gradient at w = 1 is 2(1 − 3) = −4, which is not small.
The one-step rate is 0.5; 1.1 jumps to w = 5.4.

interview.q: Explain gradient descent and the role of the learning rate.
covers: Too small crawls, too large overshoots or diverges

Metrics are what the business cares about
Choose the threshold and model with metrics

covers: Short runs on a sample at a few learning rates

mcq.q: What does vectorisation mean in NumPy?
options: Running the same Python code on a GPU instead of on the CPU
Splitting the data into small vectors by hand before each loop
Converting text into embedding vectors before any computation
Expressing computation as whole-array operations instead of Python loops
mcq.why: Whole-array operations run in fast compiled code; Python loops are typically hundreds of times slower.
distractors: NumPy runs on the CPU; vectorising means array operations in compiled code.
Splitting by hand keeps the slow Python loop.
That is embedding, not vectorised computation.

mcq.q: What is broadcasting?
options: Sending the same array to several GPUs at once for training
Printing an array's contents in a readable, aligned layout
Combining arrays of different shapes by stretching size-1 axes
Shuffling the rows of an array before each training epoch
mcq.why: For example, adding a (3, 1) array to a (1, 4) array gives a (3, 4) result.
distractors: That is replicating data across devices.
Printing has nothing to do with combining shapes.
Shuffling reorders rows; it does not combine arrays.

mcq.q: Why move code out of notebooks once it stabilises?
options: Notebooks cannot draw plots once the dataset grows past memory
Notebooks hide execution order, so results can depend on cells run out of order
Notebooks cannot import packages that were installed with pip
Modules always run faster than the same code in a notebook cell
mcq.why: Hidden state makes notebooks fragile; versioned modules run the same way each time.

mcq.q: Which of these must you pin to make an experiment reproducible? Choose all that apply.

mcq.q: Your dataset version is recorded as “data.csv”. What is wrong with that?
options: A file name is not a version; record a content hash or use a versioning tool
The name is too short to be unique across the team's projects

CSV cannot store typed data, so the version is lost when loaded
mcq.why: The file can change under the same name; a hash or a tool such as DVC pins the exact content.
distractors: A longer name is still not a version: the content can change under it.
The file can change while its name stays the same.
The format is not the problem; the name does not identify the content.

mcq.q: GPU kernels are not always bit-for-bit deterministic. What should you record?
options: The tolerance you accept between runs
Nothing; results are always identical
The time of day
Only the GPU's brand
mcq.why: Record that small differences are expected, and how large they may be.
distractors: They can differ slightly across runs.
Time of day is irrelevant.
The model, driver and library versions matter more than the brand.

mcq.q: You fit a normalisation (mean and standard deviation) on the full dataset and then split it. What is the problem?
options: It changes the labels of the test rows
It is slower than normalising after the split
Nothing, as long as the split is random
Test-set statistics leak into training
mcq.why: Fit preprocessing on the training split only, then apply it to validation and test.
distractors: Normalising features does not touch the labels.
Speed is not the problem; leakage is.
A random split after fitting still leaks test statistics.

mcq.q: About how much memory do the weights of an 8-billion-parameter model need in BF16?

About 8 GB
About 16 GB
About 32 GB

distractors: That is roughly 4-bit.
That is 1 byte per parameter (INT8 or FP8).

options: About 4–5 GB
About 32 GB
About 16 GB

distractors: That is FP32.
That is BF16.

mcq.q: Each generated token from an 8B BF16 model reads about 16 GB of weights. With 80 GB/s of memory bandwidth, what is the speed ceiling?
options: About 0.2 tokens per second
About 80 tokens per second
About 5 tokens per second
About 1,280 tokens per second

distractors: That inverts the division.

That multiplies instead of dividing.

mcq.q: Why do most LLM training and serving stacks use BF16 rather than FP16?
options: BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range, so large values do not overflow
BF16 uses 1 byte per number, half the memory of FP16
FP16 is not supported by current GPUs, so BF16 is the only option
BF16 is more precise than FP16 because it has more mantissa bits
mcq.why: FP16's largest value is about 65,504, so large activations overflow; BF16 trades precision for FP32's range.
distractors: BF16 uses 2 bytes, like FP16.
FP16 is widely supported.
BF16 has fewer mantissa bits; it trades precision for range.

Irrelevant.
